paragraphs.text: Dear elders and sisters, I'm a little late again today, it's been a busy day, but I want to share a very important message with you as we prepare for our worldwide fast tomorrow.
In April of 2011, Elder Dallin H. Oakes, now President Dallin H. Oakes, opened his general conference talk with these words, quote,
close quote.
Elder Oakes went on to teach us about the power of our desires and why we need to encourage and support righteous desires.
In preparation for zone interviews next week, I invite you to watch this remarkable sermon on how our desires actually shape our lives and determine our eternal destinies.

In my message to you today, I hope to share with you how our desires are actually created or developed. If, as President Oakes says, our desires determine our eternal destinies, then it makes sense to become very knowledgeable about how to create the kind of desires that will take us where we want to go. This way, we become the actual architects of our lives.
In a powerful little book called, Drawing on the Powers of Heaven, the author taught that quote,
close quote.

Now, this is true because our desires grow out of the thoughts we choose to cultivate. Each of us has many thoughts that cross our minds each day. Sometimes our minds are so busy with thoughts that we can actually lose sight of our true goals and purpose.

These thoughts can come from many places. We can have thoughts that we remember from our experiences in the past. We can have thoughts of the future that come from our imagination. We can have thoughts that come from outside influences, such as from friends or people trying to influence us to do something that they want us to do. We can have thoughts from the adversary. And of course, we can have thoughts that come from the Holy Spirit.

It is important that you understand that you are not your thoughts. Yes, you have thoughts, but you are not those thoughts. You can choose to discard them or to focus on them. That is your choice because of your agency.

We often think of agency as a time to choose between this action or that action. But it is really about choosing which thoughts to dwell on and encourage and which thoughts to refuse and discard. Since you are not your thoughts, you have this power to stand outside of your thoughts and examine them.
You can have a thought and then ask yourself this question. Does this thought build up my faith in Christ? Or does it reduce my faith?
Or you might ask this question, does this thought have the power to take me someplace I really want to be? Or will it take me away from my deepest desire?

There are other questions you could ask about any thought that you might have. But the main point I want you to understand is that you must maintain the status of being the inspector of your thoughts.

If you think of your mind as a garden and as you as an expert gardener, then you will see what I mean. Weeds grow amongst the flowers and the vegetables and as a good gardener, you will be quick to spot a weed and pull it out and put it in the trash. You will then want to plant a seed of a thought in the place where you pulled out the weed so something worthwhile and powerful can grow in that space in your garden.

As we cultivate righteous thoughts and discard unrighteous thoughts, the desires of our heart become more pure and holy. We think less about ourselves and more about others. We focus on what God wants and not just on what we want. In this process, we align ourselves with God's purposes and can therefore with confidence call upon heaven for power to come down and protect us and prosper us.
In Proverbs 23:7, we are told, as a man thinketh in his heart, so is he.

The writer of that verse is saying this same thing. He is saying that when you cultivate a thought, when you focus on it and encourage it by allowing it to stay present in your mind, it is basically like you are no longer thinking with your brain, but now you are thinking with your heart. You are saying, I want this thought to be real.

Now you could say this is a true desire of your heart, but make no mistake. You put it there through your focus on it and encouragement of it, even of those fearful negative thoughts. You say, well, not me. I don't want those things. Well, you may say you don't want them, but when you keep focusing on them, when you keep thinking about them, you are basically saying in your heart, I want this. That's why I'm focusing on it. It's a sad truth, but it's a real truth.

The unfortunate fact is that it is easier to focus on fearful and negative thoughts than it is to focus on and encourage positive and uplifting thoughts. I think this is just part of being in a fallen world where everything seems to go downhill by nature, but our work in mortality is to push back on nature.
In fact, President Brigham Young, the second president of the church, and probably one of the greatest missionaries of all time, wrote this, quote,
close quote.
Brigham Young is teaching us that though it's hard, it is the main reason we're here on this earth to learn how to manage our thoughts and bring them into harmony with the Savior.

To be an effective missionary, a person has to choose to cultivate the thoughts that bring about missionary desires in the heart. Alma expressed those desires and so did Ammon and many others throughout our scriptural record.

In each case, these righteous missionaries became filled with righteous desires because they chose to manage their thoughts and nourish those thoughts that built the correct desires in their hearts. They did this even though they were sometimes in prison and sometimes very sick and many times walked and ridiculed by the very people they were trying to help.

Now why should we think that it would be any different for us than it was for them? If it is our goal to be like the Savior, then we have to begin to think like Him so that we can begin to desire the things that He has desired and thereby act like He acts. I testify that this is true and that as you cultivate righteous thoughts, you will grow the righteous desires in your heart that will carry you back into the presence of God.

Well, tomorrow, as I said at the beginning, President Russell M. Nelson has invited us to participate in a worldwide fast to lessen the effects of this virus. I hope you are all planning on participating in this fast. We do need the help. I want to remind you though to drink water, stay hydrated.

The most important aspect of the fast is what you think about. As we have been discussing in this message, our thoughts are what drive our desires and our destinies. As we are fasting, if all we are doing is going without food while we are thinking about worldly things, we might as well not bother fasting because it isn't doing much good.

If however, we are mindful of the purpose of the fast throughout the day and we do as the Prophet Joseph Smith taught in the lectures on faith, that faith is mental exertion, not physical force. Mentally exerting ourselves means that when we fast, we should be mentally focusing on the outcome we are hoping for in our fast. So be mindful of the outcome you want as you fast tomorrow.

Elders and sisters, I'm looking forward to zone interviews starting on Monday. I've missed being able to see you in a regular way. But these zone interviews will be a little different, but they will be good. I'll enjoy visiting with you over that video feed and I know that we'll be edified together.

Sister Hughes and I love you. We pray for you every day. We're excited to see the growth that you're going through and the tremendous proactivity that many of you are demonstrating as you're doing this work in these difficult circumstances.
Make it a great evening. Get a good night's rest so that you can really focus on the Sabbath tomorrow. God bless you. Good night.
